name: The Winstons
hook: A Washington soul band whose drummer's six-second solo on a B-side became the most famous drum break in the world.
blurb: The Winstons were a soul band from Washington, D.C. Their 1969 hit 'Color Him Father' won a Grammy for its writer, the saxophonist Richard Spencer. On the other side of the single was 'Amen, Brother', where the drummer Gregory Coleman plays a drum solo about six seconds long. Hip-hop producers sampled it, and then in the 1990s British jungle and drum and bass producers chopped it up and sped it up until it was the sound of a whole genre. It is called the Amen break, and it is the defining case of a sample becoming bigger than the record it came from. Its jump into British dance music, its clearest crossing between lineages, runs through Shy FX's 'Original Nuttah' (1994), the first jungle or drum and bass record to chart in Britain. Spencer, who held the copyright, never got paid for any of its thousands of uses. In 2015 two British DJs raised about 24,000 pounds for him online, a goodwill gesture, not a settlement. Coleman, who played it, is reported to have died in 2006 without recognition.
